chapter: Al Hibbler, Dakota Staton and later years
title: The late, drunk driver of Dakota's station wagon
summary: After twelve hours' wait the chauffeur shows up, begins swerving, and Malachi takes the wheel for the drive east.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: What seemed like might have been a question as to whether I would really leave or not was really confirmed when we were on our way back from Chicago to New York. Because the guy that had been driving the station wagon that belonged to Dakota, he was kind of the valet and chauffeur and whatever, and he handled all the instruments... He had been hanging out the night that we closed, and we were supposed to leave the next day, at something like 2 o'clock the next afternoon after closing. The Roberts Show Lounge, that was the name of the club that we played. At 2 o'clock, the time we were supposed to leave, he was nowhere in sight. Of course, Dakota and her husband had taken a plane back to New York; we were to drive in the station wagon. A very nice car, so it was comfortable and everything.
Anyway, we waited for this guy, 2 o'clock, 3 o'clock and so on, up into the night. Finally, he didn't show up until

somewhere like around 11 o'clock that night. He had been out somewhere having himself a ball, and one would assume that, along with other things, a young lady must have been involved. Anyway, he came in and he's making all sorts of apologies about not being back on time -- because we had been waiting around there for almost 12 hours for him. Because we wanted to leave! It was expensive, because when you do something like that you either hang out in a bar, or you spend money or you're doing something... You might even wind up gambling or something.

But he came, and we got things in the station wagon, and took off for New York from Chicago. He was driving. And before we got to Indiana, he started playing tricks with the lines on the road. And I noticed it, and of course, everybody else did. So we gave him a good tongue-lashing, and I told him, 'Man, get the hell out from under the wheel. Because you're in no shape to drive.' And he didn't give me any argument at all, because he naturally wanted to rest. So before I had been driving ten minutes, he was in the back of the station wagon, snoring like he'd been asleep for five hours.
